was looking into this and noticed a couple of things about [test_stream_timeout](https://github.com/psf/requests/blob/main/tests/test_requests.py#L2537-L2541) that make me think that it may be redundant.\n\n1. When that test was [introduced](https://github.com/psf/requests/pull/1935) it was the first, and only test of timeouts in the test suite. It seems to be named that way because it was added when the handling for timeouts on requests where the `stream` parameter is `True`, but the test isn't actually setting `stream=True`. The accompanying code change actually removed a branch in the timeout handling code - it used to only set connect timeouts when stream was true, but after the change, it set both connect and read timeouts regardless of the value of stream. So really, this test is just testing read timeouts.\n\n1. The next thing to notice is that now there are a lot more tests around timeouts, and today we have [test_read_timeout](https://github.com/psf/requests/blob/main/tests/test_requests.py#L2568-L2576) which runs the other 2 tests that use the `delay/10` httbin endpoint that's causing the slow tests. I'm pretty sure that's effectively testing the same thing as `test_stream_timeout`. The `test_read_timeout` calls both set the connect timeout to None and only test read timeouts, where the `test_stream_timeout` call is using a scalar so both connect and read timeouts are set to the same value, but the test is written to succeed when it returns an exception with \"Read timed out\" in the args.\n\n1. The final nail in the coffin for test_stream_timeout is that the way that test is written, it will actually pass the test (false positive) if the request succeeds without timing out. If you look at how all of the other timeout tests are written, there's a `pytest.fail()` after the get request that's supposed to time out - so if the exception doesn't get raised, the test fails. That's not there on `test_stream_timeout`, so if the exception doesn't happen, the test completes and doesn't record a failure.\n\n1. The only case that I can see where `test_stream_timeout` is doing anything that's not currently covered by one of the other tests is testing that using a simple scalar type for the timeout parameter is accepted. We can add that test to `test_total_timeout_connect` which doesn't use httpbin.\n\nIt also looks like httbin `delay` allows floating point values, not just integers. Initially, these tests were all configured to run across the internet to `httpbin.org` so I think the `delay/10` that was originally chosen made sense because the internet connection might be slow or flaky during tests and allowing for a longer test window might have made the tests more reliable, but as the tests now run locally, that should be less of a concern. The 10 second delay also was being borne by the server and didn't have any impact on the test suite's execution speed - which was only bound by the local timeout. I feel like we could probably reliably switch it to `delay/0.25` so the httbin server would only block for 250ms twice. That seems like it should be long enough to reliably run a test that should time out in 100ms - but we could even drop the timeout parameter to 0.05 - and make it a 50msec timeout against an endpoint that lasts 250ms for a bit more buffer.\n\nWhile we're at it, we can DRY up the repeated `0.1` parameter everywhere and make all of the timeouts consistently faster.\n\nHere's my proposed
